articles.body: La sonrisa de Carlos Alcaraz mueve montañas. Su imagen fresca, su carácter extrovertido y su condición de ganador, le reportan millones con independencia de que las lesiones le dejen un tiempo sin jugar. Según la revista Forbes, el tenista de El Palmar es el que más dinero ha acumulado fuera de las pistas el último año, en patrocinadores y exhibiciones, con un total de unos 38 millones de dólares. Sus resultados deportivos le reportaron 15,7 millones. Alcaraz es imagen de Nike, que le renovó con un contrato de superestrella, Babolat, Rolex, Itaú, BMW, Isdin, ElPozo, Louis Vuitton y Grupo Danone, entre otros. Es un fijo desde hace dos años en la Laver Cup, competición organizada por la empresa de Roger Federer, y en el lucrativo Six Kings Slam de Ryad (Arabia Saudí). El mes de diciembre pasado disputó dos exhibiciones, en New Jersey contra Frances Tiafoe, y Miami frente a Joao Fonseca. En enero jugó en Corea del Sur, con Jannik Sinner como acompañante. La pasión que desprende Carlitos entre los aficionados se demuestra en el hecho que el pasado mes de octubre se pagó 173.000 dólares por una de las raquetas que utilizó en la final de Wimbledon 2023, el que fue el primero de sus dos títulos seguidos sobre la hierba del All England Club. Jannik Sinner, actualmente en el primero puesto del ranking y campeón de cinco grandes, entre ellos el último Wimbledon, es segundo en ese ranking, con 35 millones de dólares. A esos hay que sumar 23 más con la raqueta. Serena Williams, que ha estado retirada hasta el pasado mes de junio cuando reapareció en el dobles de Queen's, acumula 40,1 millones de dólares generados fuera del circuito profesional. De hecho, ella se retiró oficialmente de las pistas en 2022 tras la derrota en la tercera ronda del US Open ante Ajla Tomljanovic.

articles.title: 'Sometimes I forget that I'm also kind of famous': Alex Eala is rewriting tennis stardom at US Open 2026
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: No sooner had Alexandra Eala closed out her second-round match on Louis Armstrong Stadium than a rush of activity erupted on the rear d.
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: No sooner had Alexandra Eala closed out her second-round match on Louis Armstrong Stadium than a rush of activity erupted on the rear deck of the packed arena. Feet shuffled, voices rose and squeals rang out as young fans, most of them little girls in tennis attire clutching giant tennis balls, raced down the stairs, desperate to get as close to the Filipina as possible for an autograph.Eala, 21, needed just 64 minutes to beat Ukraine’s Oleksandra Oliynykova 6-1, 6-4 and reach the third round of the US Open, her deepest run in New York.Yet at a career-high No. 18 in the world, the highest for a Southeast Asian in WTA history, Eala’s following appears to be growing faster than her resume. The first Filipino to defeat top-10 opponents, reach the semifinals of a WTA 1000 event, win a WTA Tour title and make the fourth round at a major.While her achievements are path-breaking her popularity is something else entirely.Having reached the second round on her US Open main-draw debut last year, Eala showed how much she has grown, both in temperament and tennis, striking 19 winners while refusing to dance to Oliynykova’s tune, no matter how often the Ukrainian changed pace and spin.Thursday’s result was sweet revenge for Eala, who had lost to the 25-year-old four months ago on clay in Strasbourg.The Ukrainian, an orthodox player, pushed against the run of play and the weight of the crowd in the second set, but Eala stood firm to close out the win. In the stands, fans filmed the closing stages on their phones, turning themselves into broadcasters of sorts as they provided live commentary for an audience back home.In the third round on Saturday, she’ll go up against good friend the No. 14 seed Iva Jovic.Eala’s rapidly growing commercial portfolio includes global giants and leading Philippine brands, yet her real currency may be the crowds she commands. Almost everywhere she goes, Filipino fans turn up in force, reshaping the atmosphere around her matches and turning Eala into something tennis rarely produces, a star whose appeal transcends the sport itself.Her popularity has become impossible for tournaments to ignore. Some have been criticised for putting the world No. 18 on smaller courts, with too few seats for her fans, while even her practice sessions at Flushing Meadows have attracted fans willing to line up just to watch her. New York City is home to an estimated 94,000 Filipinos with more than half living in the Queens borough which is also home to the US Open.Eala then was back on the second-biggest court at Flushing Meadows for the second time in as many outings on Thursday, while Grand Slam champions like six-time major winner and former No.1 Iga Swiatek, American Madison Keys and reigning Roland Garros champion Mirra Andreeva played their second round matches on smaller courts.Eala shrugged. “I don’t control the scheduling,” she said.She doesn’t.Should a player’s popularity influence their standing in the sport, or should that be determined by the silverware they have stacked up? It makes for a lively debate.Tennis is a highly individualistic sport, its biggest stars, read most successful, defining the eras they play in.But the rise of social media in an age of relentless self-expression has changed the equation. A player’s reach, influence and celebrity can now rival their results, raising an intriguing question, is the individual more important than the sport?Asked about her meeting with media personality Ornella Rose Hollela in New York last week, Eala called the interaction “super crazy”, saying it all happened too fast.“It's weird that some people that I watch a lot, they know me,” Eala said before adding, “Sometimes I forget that I'm also kind of famous.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Career turning point: “I’m not a Serena fan. I’m just a tennis player”: How Naomi Osaka’s emotional US Open win over Serena Williams changed her career forever, making her a global star
articles.summary: International Sports News: Naomi Osaka arrived at the 2018 US Open as a talented 20-year-old who had already shown she could trouble the biggest names in tennis. What happened i.
articles.body: Naomi Osaka arrived at the 2018 US Open as a talented 20-year-old who had already shown she could trouble the biggest names in tennis. What happened in New York, however, turned her from a rising star into a Grand Slam champion.Her 6-2, 6-4 victory over Serena Williams in the final was more than Osaka’s first major title. It became the defining moment of her career and the match that introduced her to a global audience in a way no previous result had done.How did beating Serena Williams become Naomi Osaka’s career turning point?The signs that Osaka was ready for a major breakthrough had already appeared earlier in 2018. She won her first WTA title at Indian Wells, beating Daria Kasatkina 6-3, 6-2 in the final after defeating Maria Sharapova, Agnieszka Radwanska, Karolina Pliskova and world No. 1 Simona Halep during the tournament. The run pushed her into the world’s top 25 and gave her the confidence to believe she could compete with the best players on the biggest stages.The US Open, though, presented a completely different challenge. Osaka entered the tournament as the No. 20 seed and reached her first Grand Slam final without dropping a set in the semifinal against Madison Keys. She beat the American 6-2, 6-4 and saved all 13 break points she faced, becoming the first Japanese woman in the Open Era to reach a Grand Slam singles final.Waiting for her was Serena, the player Osaka had admired since childhood. Osaka had never hidden what Serena meant to her. Before the final, she explained that she had dreamed about facing Williams on a Grand Slam stage since she was a child. Yet she also understood that treating the final like a fan could make the occasion overwhelming, so she tried to separate her admiration from the task in front of her.“Even when I was a little kid, I always dreamed that I would play Serena in a final of a Grand Slam,” Osaka said before the match.She then added, “At the same time I feel like even though I should enjoy this moment, I should still think of it as another match. I shouldn't really think of her as my idol. I should just try to play her as an opponent.”That approach showed immediately. Osaka played with remarkable control, breaking Serena early in the first set and refusing to allow the occasion to dictate her tennis. She won the opening set 6-2 and carried that momentum into the second.The final became increasingly tense because of the controversy surrounding Serena and chair umpire Carlos Ramos. Williams received a code violation for coaching, followed by a point penalty after breaking her racquet and a game penalty after being assessed a verbal abuse violation. The situation created a hostile atmosphere inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, but Osaka continued trying to stay focused on the match.She eventually closed it out 6-2, 6-4 on her second championship point.The credentials showed just how composed she had been. Osaka hit six aces, saved five of six break points and converted four of five break opportunities against Williams. More importantly, she never allowed the drama around the court to pull her completely away from the job.That was what made the victory such a major turning point. Osaka did not simply beat one of the greatest players in tennis. She handled the pressure of playing her childhood idol, the weight of a Grand Slam final and an increasingly emotional atmosphere, all before turning 21.After the match, Osaka famously said, “When I step onto the court, I feel like a different person. I’m not a Serena fan. I’m just a tennis player playing another tennis player. But then when I hugged her at the net, I felt like a little kid again.”That quote captured the strange reality of the night. On the court, Osaka had played Serena as an opponent. At the net, she was still the young girl who had grown up watching her.How did the 2018 US Open change Naomi Osaka’s career?The title immediately changed Osaka’s position in tennis. Before New York, she was a promising young player with one WTA title. After New York, she was a Grand Slam champion and one of the biggest names in the sport.She also became the first Japanese player, male or female, to win a Grand Slam singles title. That achievement gave her a place in Japanese tennis history while also establishing her as one of the leading players of her generation.The victory over Serena was not an isolated success either. Osaka followed it by winning the 2019 Australian Open, where she defeated Petra Kvitova in the final. That second major title made her the first Japanese player to reach the No. 1 ranking in the WTA rankings.Her rise continued at the 2020 US Open. Osaka defeated Victoria Azarenka in the final after recovering from a set and a break down to claim her third Grand Slam title. In 2021, she won the Australian Open again, beating Jennifer Brady in the final for her fourth major championship.That sequence changed the way Osaka was viewed. The 2018 US Open was no longer simply a surprising breakthrough. It became the beginning of a period in which she established herself as a genuine Grand Slam force.Her success also gave her a much larger platform away from tennis. Osaka became one of the most recognizable athletes in the world, with her public profile growing alongside her results. Her willingness to speak openly about pressure, expectations and life away from the court also made her a prominent figure far beyond tennis.Yet the significance of the 2018 final goes deeper than the trophies that followed. It showed Osaka that she could handle a moment that looked almost impossibly large. She was facing a player she had idolized, in front of a packed New York crowd, with her first Grand Slam title within reach. Instead of allowing the occasion to overwhelm her, she trusted the tennis that had taken her there.Osaka herself later reflected on how quickly her life changed after winning Indian Wells and then the US Open. In 2026, she recalled that after Indian Wells she thought life could not get much crazier because the victory had helped her mother retire. Then the US Open brought another level of change.That progression helps explain why New York remains such an important part of her career story. Indian Wells proved Osaka could beat elite players. The US Open proved she could do it when everything around the match became enormous.Why does Serena Williams remain central to Naomi Osaka’s career story?Serena’s importance to Osaka’s story did not disappear after that final. If anything, the match created a connection between the two players that became part of Osaka’s identity.The most striking part was how Osaka viewed Serena even after becoming the person who had defeated her in a Grand Slam final. The result did not erase the admiration she had carried since childhood.“The thing is, I don't know what happened on the court. So for me, I'm always going to remember the Serena that I love,” Osaka said after the final. “It doesn't change anything for me.”That sentiment explained why the victory was so emotional for her. Osaka had achieved the dream she had once imagined as a young fan, but the person standing across the net was still someone she respected deeply.At the same time, Osaka understood that beating Serena meant she had to create her own identity. She later put that balance into simple words: “She’ll always be someone I look up to. But tennis-wise, I want to try to do my own thing. I want to be my own person.”That became an important theme of Osaka’s career. She was no longer simply the player who admired Serena Williams. She had become a champion with her own place in tennis.Still, when looking for the single moment that changed the direction of her career, the answer remains clear. Indian Wells announced Osaka to the tennis world, but the 2018 US Open final changed her status forever.She entered Arthur Ashe Stadium as a 20-year-old playing her childhood idol. She left it as a Grand Slam champion and the first Japanese player to win a major singles title. The controversy surrounding the final became part of its history, but Osaka’s tennis was what ultimately defined the night.Hence, the 2018 US Open remains the clearest career turning point for Naomi Osaka. It was the night she stopped being the promising young player everyone was watching and became the champion everyone had to watch.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The presence of influencers and tennis etiquette become hot topics at the US Open
articles.summary: Naomi Osaka usually does not have a problem focusing on playing tennis and blocking out the crowd when she's on the court.  “There was a moment where there w...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Naomi Osaka usually does not have a problem focusing on playing tennis and blocking out the crowd when she's on the court. Her first-round match at the U.S. Open became a notable exception.

"There was a moment where there was people shouting and stuff," Osaka said. "You could hear it quite clearly."

The source of the disruption: a group of influencers and content creators who have been afforded widespread access at this U.S. Open. The number of content creators who were credentialed to cover the tournament has doubled from last year, and the interruptions have made the influencers and tennis etiquette a hot topic at Flushing Meadows.

Chair umpire Kader Nouni admonished a group of influencers in a suite for recording a video in the middle of a point, and another incident Monday night involved the use of a bright ring light to take photos. In Osaka's second match, chair umpire Marijana Veljovic asked fans several times to be quiet, an effort the players appreciated.

"It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like first-round match," Osaka said Thursday after advancing to the third round . "Overall, I think there is huge positives. ... You want people to continue to grow the sport. I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."

The U.S. Tennis Association began inviting creators last year, and spokesperson Brendan McIntyre said reaching new audiences is essential to the growth of the sport and the U.S. Open.

There have been some crowd and noise hiccups, including again Thursday when Osaka played Katerina Siniakova.

"Sometimes the people don't realize that even when they're like up and they are talking, you can hear it down (on the court)," Siniakova said. "You just don't think about it. You think: 'Oh, I'm somewhere where no one even, like, hears me, but it's not really true. Actually, in this big stadium, it's everything, is going everywhere."

Arthur Ashe Stadium, which serves as center court, has emerged as the place to be at the U.S. Open — often with the famous Honey Deuce cocktail and its tennis ball-shaped melons in hand. It has become common for fans to pose for photos in the middle of matches while play is ongoing.

"Sometimes it's their first tennis match; they don't know. They have probably been to basketball games before," 2023 champion Coco Gauff said, wondering if brands that invite influencers should put up etiquette signs as a way of helping. "With anything, any venue you go to, if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans. I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport."

Madison Appel, a college tennis player at Indiana who teaches lessons as a coach and is an influencer, responded to the criticism on TikTok and Instagram by giving her own tips for those unfamiliar with how to act at matches.

"The problem is not the influencer: The problem is that no one understands tennis etiquette," Appel said. "You should only be walking around and taking photos when the two players are sitting down, the music's up and it's lively. When players are playing, and they're in between serving games, you should be in your seat, not taking photos and keeping it quiet. When a player is ready to serve, everyone needs to respect that, sit down and just watch."

Earlier this week, video screens began displaying a message to "Please refrain from the use of flash photography and other lighting." Osaka notices the noise more than the lights, while Gauff is most concerned about flash photography.

They and other players have mixed feelings about influencers. Daniil Medvedev, ranked eighth in the world in men's singles, is all for making tennis more popular and joked that one downside is getting recognized by more people on the street or at restaurants.

"If it disturbs during the play, like if you see the light or something, well, you always say to the referee, can be sometimes challenging, like if during the point this happens," Medvedev said. "But I'm pretty sure as well, even them, maybe one time they do it, and then someone tells them not to do it. (There is) a lot of more upside than downside, so go for it."

Frances Tiafoe does not see much of a downside to more butts in seats, with the goal of getting fans from all walks of life into tennis. Fellow American Jessica Pegula sees a benefit to influencers showcasing the U.S. Open experience but wonders if there's a tipping point.

"It's tough when you see videos like that when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights," Pegula said. "People are down there trying to perform, and it's their career and their job. It seems like a bit disrespectful. I think it's gotten a little maybe too much, it feels like, this year. I don't know. I think I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."

articles.summary: Aryna Sabalenka beats Kamilla Rakhimova 6-3 6-4, despite complaints of cannabis smell in first set; Carlos Alcaraz also comes through in straight sets, beating Wu Yibing 6-3 6-4 6-1; watch US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, on NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The world No 1 came through in straight sets, beating her unseeded opponent 6-3 6-4 on Louis Armstrong Stadium, but after racing into a 3-0 lead in the opening set, Sabalenka complained to umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore at the first changeover.

"I was like, 'Guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please to not do it around ‌the tennis courts'," Sabalenka told reporters afterwards. "It's a bit tricky to handle that smell while you're trying to compete at your best."

No fans were found to be smoking and ejected from the tennis grounds.

Sabalenka added: "I don't know if it was coming from the crowd or was from the outside, because the wind blows it into the stadium. I don't know. I just hope they're going to be a bit more aware of that stuff."

US Tennis Association spokesman Brendan McIntyre said in a statement: "While we can't control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this facility as a smoke free environment."

The distraction didn't affect Sabalenka's form in the slightest as she didn't miss a single first serve until the seventh game of the match, in which Rakhimova would three times take her to deuce.

That would prove to be Rakhimova's only real opening in the first set, Sabalenka taking it 6-3, but she'd prove much more competitive in the second.

Rakhimova came from behind four-straight times to hold serve, saving four break points along the way, before Sabalenka finally ended her resolve in the ninth game of the second set.

On this occasion, Rakhimova let a 40-0 lead slip as the four-time Grand Slam champion battled back to secure the crucial break before serving things out to book her spot in the last 16.

Sabalenka 'shuts down outside noise' to book Townsend meeting

After Sabalenka's second-round win, she cut short questions about her pre-tournament activities in an excruciating exchange with a reporter.

A regular poster on social media at the various events she attends and with the brands she works, Sabalenka fired back that her off-court appearances had not come at the expense of her preparations ​for Flushing Meadows.

Referencing that further after her victory over Rakhimova, Sabalenka added: "I completely shut down noise from outside.

"I focus on myself, and I know if I do that and work really hard I will have my chances and be able to play a great level of tennis."

Trying to become the first player to win three-straight US Open titles since Serena Williams from 2012-14, Sabalenka will face American Taylor Townsend in the last 16 after she beat 13th seed Diana Shnaider 6-2 6-7 (3-7) 6-3

Jessica Pegula kept alive her bid ‌for a maiden Grand Slam title when the third seed rallied from behind ‌to beat fellow former US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez 1-6 ​6-4 6-3.

The American will face Romania's Sorana Cirstea ​in the last 16 after the 16th seed defeated Italy Jasmine Paolini in straight sets 6-3 6-3.

Alcaraz overcomes mid-match wobble to reach fourth round

Defending men's champion Carlos Alcaraz continued his impressive comeback after more than four months out to a wrist injury, as he beat Wu Yibing in straight sets, 6-3 6-4 6-1, on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The seven-time Grand Slam champion was made to work harder than the scoreline suggests, however, as he was broken back in both the first two sets by his 113th-ranked opponent.

The second set, in particular, was cause for frustration for the Spaniard as he appeared to be cruising along at 2-0 up after winning five games in a row, only to again be pegged back by Wu.

Alcaraz would finally earn another break of serve in the 10th game to clinch a two-set lead before he finally pulled clear in the third.

"In the toughest moments I did everything good, which I'm really happy about," Alcaraz said in his on-court interview. "Could it be better? Yes. But overall I'm just really proud and happy with the performance today.

"To be honest, I'm playing better than I thought [after wrist injury]. Physically, I thought I was going to be dead after the first match. But I'm recovering really well.

"My level right now is really good, I've got the rhythm of the competition every time I step on the court."

Alcaraz will face American 20th seed Tommy Paul ‌ in the last 16 after he emerged victorious from a five-set thriller against Kazakhstan's 15th seed Alexander Bublik, winning 6-4 3-6 6-7 (4-7) 6-1 6-3 in a match that lasted three hours and 13 minutes.

Elsewhere, seventh seed, and 2021 US Open champion, Daniil Medvedev overpowered Frenchman Arthur ‌Rinderknech with a 6-4 6-4 6-4 victory.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka's win over Kamilla Rakhimova interrupted by cannabis smell
articles.summary: Aryna Sabalenka briefly halts her US Open match against Kamilla Rakhimova because of the smell of cannabis before going on to reach the fourth round.
articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka briefly halted her US Open match against Kamilla Rakhimova because of a strong smell of cannabis before cruising into the fourth round in New York.

Top seed Sabalenka raised the issue after going 3-0 up in the first set against Uzbekistan's Rakhimova, telling umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore that "someone is smoking weed".

The Belarusian asked the umpire to intervene "because it's so strong".

Asderaki-Moore spoke to an official on her radio and made a smoking gesture to someone behind her, before play continued.

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka went on to secure a confident 6-3 6-4 victory on Louis Armstrong Stadium as she chases a fifth Grand Slam singles title.

Sabalenka said afterwards she was not sure where the smell of cannabis was coming from but asked fans to be more mindful.

Smoking is not permitted on site at Flushing Meadows but the smell of cannabis sometimes wafts on to court from the nearby Corona Park.

It is legal to smoke it in New York for adults aged 21 and over.

"It's a bit tricky to handle that smell while you're trying to compete at your best," Sabalenka said.

"I don't know if it was coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium.

"I just hope they're going to be a bit more aware of that stuff."

Sabalenka is not the first player at this year's US Open to complain about the smell of cannabis at Flushing Meadows.

Britain's Katie Boulter previously said it was distracting, while Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones also noticed the smell.

In past years players including Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev have also complained.

Victory marked Sabalenka's 16th straight win at Flushing Meadows as she bids to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2012-2014 to complete a hat-trick of US Open singles titles.

The 28-year-old showcased her trademark power from the start against Rakhimova, dropping just four points on serve in a confident opening set.

Although Rakhimova fought well in the second set, Sabalenka secured the crucial break to go 5-4 up before safely serving out victory.

Sabalenka served 10 aces to Rakhimova's two and did not face a single break point.

She will face crowd favourite Taylor Townsend for a place in the quarter-finals after the American beat Russian 15th seed Diana Shnaider 6-2 6-7 (3-7) 6-3.

'I was a little lazy to start off' - Pegula battles through

American third seed Jessica Pegula kept her bid for a first Grand Slam title alive by coming from a set down to beat Leylah Fernandez.

Pegula, who lost the final at Flushing Meadows two years ago to Sabalenka, came through 1-6 6-4 6-3 against the Canadian 31st seed.

Fernandez showed glimpses of the form that took her to the 2021 US Open final, where she lost to Emma Raducanu, as she raced through the first set in under 30 minutes.

But Pegula played with more patience to secure the decisive break at the end of the second set - albeit with some help from a net cord.

She saved two break points at the start of the deciding set, before breaking in the next game and going on to see out victory with a backhand volley.

"I wasn't moving my feet up to the ball, and I was a little lazy to start off," Pegula, 32, said.

"I was going to have to dig deep. I'm glad I was able to find somewhere there in the second set to turn it around."

Pegula will play Romanian 16th seed Sorana Cirstea in the fourth round after she beat Italian 19th seed Jasmine Paolini 6-3 6-3.

Última hora del Alcaraz - Wu en directo:

Buenas tardes, bienvenidos a la quinta jornada del US Open 2026. Hoy volvemos a tener en pista a Carlos Alcaraz, luchando por un puesto en la segunda semana del torneo. Flushing Meadows está preparada para recibir a los protagonistas de hoy: el fenómeno de El Palmar, con 16 victorias de Grand Slam consecutivas a sus espaldas, ante el chino Yibing Wu, campeón de un título ATP 250 en Dallas. El encuentro se disputará en el segundo turno de la Arthur Ashe, alrededor de las 19:30 h en Nueva York.

Carlos Alcaraz llega con grandes sensaciones. Tras imponerse con claridad en sus dos primeras pruebas desde la lesión, el murciano está a solo un partido de alcanzar la segunda semana en el grande neoyorkino. Ya conserva, de momento, la segunda mejor marca de la historia en porcentaje de victorias en torneos de Grand Slam con un 87,74%, solo es superado por el sueco Björn Borg (89,91%). Para llegar hasta aquí, pasó por encima del ruso Safiullin en su debut y tiró de galones para remontar al portugués Jaime Faria.

Por su parte, Wu, de 26 años y en el puesto 113 del ranking, llega sin ceder sets. En la ronda inicial derrotó con firmeza al australiano Adam Walton y mejoró su rendimiento ante James Duckworth. Se trata de un deportista histórico para el país asiático, tras convertirse en el primer tenista chino en levantar un título ATP. Fue en Dallas, ante el americano John Isner.

Existe un único precedente entre ambos tenistas. Se cerró con la victoria de Alcaraz por 7-6 (5) y 6-3 en el Masters 1000 de Shanghái 2024. El campeón de siete grandes busca seguir su mágica estela en La Gran Manzana.

articles.body:
Unranked Taylor Townsend upset No. 15 Diana Shnaider 6-2, 6-7, 6-3 on Friday to advance to the fourth round at the U.S. Open for the second straight year.

Townsend came close to closing out the match in the second set, but Shnaider broke while Townsend was serving for the win. The 30-year-old American rebounded in the final set to close out Shnaider.

It's the third time Townsend has reached the fourth round at a Grand Slam event with all three times coming at the U.S. Open.

A trip to Flushing Meadows has helped Townsend the past two Grand Slam seasons. The U.S. Open is the only major tournament where she's advanced beyond the first round since 2023.

Townsend will next face No. 1 seed and reigning back-to-back U.S. Open champion Aryna Sabalenka, who defeated Kamilla Rakhimova on Friday .

articles.title: US Open: How influencers have sparked debate at Flushing Meadows as Naomi Osaka, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula have their say
articles.summary: Influencers and content creators causing disruptions at the US Open have led to leading players having their say on tennis etiquette at Flushing Meadows; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The number of content creators who have been accredited to cover this year's final Grand Slam of the year has doubled from last year in a move by organisers to reach new audiences. Yet the noise and disturbance caused by them in the stands as been felt by players on court.

Chair umpire Kader Nouni admonished a group of influencers in a suite for recording a video in the middle of a point, while another incident saw a creator using the use of a bright portable ring light to take photos.

Meanwhile, in Naomi Osaka's second-round victory, chair umpire Marijana Veljovic asked fans several times to be quiet.

Some players have questioned whether the push for online engagement has gone too far with two-time champion Osaka saying: "I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport.".

"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette."

The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning spectators no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.

And since Osaka's opening match, there has been increased messaging on screens reminding people to refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights.

American and third seed Jessica Pegula has said some of the behaviour has been "disrespectful".

"I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," she said. "But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.

"People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful."

Celebrities have long been ubiquitous in the stands - from A-list stars to US President Donald Trump - as the ultra-wealthy shell out thousands of dollars for seats to get through Flushing Meadows' doors.

But the growing love affair between influencers and the premier ⁠American tennis event has caused some growing pains.

World No 4 Coco Gauff welcomed the influx of new fans but said they should respect the traditions of tennis.

"I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," she said.

"But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans.

"I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport."

Eliza Wastcoat is an influencer who has a passion and knowledge for tennis. She has even launched her own social media channel exploring the intersection of tennis and fashion.

Wastcoat, who moved to America to attend the prestigious Lehigh University, and began her professional career at a creative agency, believes there is room to grow the game but only if organisers and influencers can work together.

"There is a space in tennis for influencers and content creators to be welcomed into the sport and reach new audiences, but I think there's ways in which the sport can do that which includes content creators and influencers who appreciate the sport itself and the etiquette of it and for those who are maybe new and are bringing new audiences in," said Wastcoat, who served as a Wimbledon ball kid when she was younger.

"I do think it's the responsibility of both the brands, the tournaments and the individuals coming to read up a little bit and understand the etiquette of the type of sporting event they're going to.

"Tennis has really opened up its doors to change but ultimately players need some quiet and the ability to concentrate.

"We all want tennis to grow so inviting people in and making it an all-round experience is great for the game, so it's just an opportunity to further educate people about the game on what tennis is."

The United States Tennis Association said it wanted fans to have an "incredible time" while ensuring they did not interfere with the action.

"We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited," read a statement from the governing body.

Wastcoat said it's also a learning curve for the USTA, adding: "What's the balance of how many credentials or tickets do we give to folks who are new, or how many do we give to creators who know and appreciate the sport? It's trying to find that balance.

"Experiences like this show that tennis is increasing in popularity so in the end more people are going to be a part of it. There's more opportunity with brands than there ever has been and I expect that to continue."

articles.standfirst: El murciano, verdugo de Wu en tres sets, pasa con nota sus tres primeros partidos tras su regreso
articles.summary: El murciano, verdugo de Wu en tres sets, pasa con nota sus tres primeros partidos tras su regreso
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz ya está en octavos de final del US Open tras superar a Yibing Wu (6-3, 6-4 y 6-1), lo que significa haber superado la primera semana de competición en el cuarto Grand Slam del calendario. Era el primer objetivo para un tenista que reconoció aterrizar en Nueva York con la única expectativa de volver a competir y acabar sano y que ahora ya vislumbra a lo lejos el gran botín. Alcaraz, después de 139 días alejado de la competición oficial, necesitaba un rodaje. Roman Safiullin, Jaime Faria y Wu se lo han dado. Los buenos son más peligrosos a partir de las rondas finales y la cuarta ya es una de ellas. El balance es un set cedido y la sensación de que puede pegarle a la pelota con total libertad a pesar de jugar con la malla protectora en su brazo derecho. Wu, el primer chino que ganó un título ATP en Dallas 2023, es un jugador "de videojuegos", según Samuel López, entrenador del campeón de siete 'majors'. El murciano ha vuelto con las mismas costumbres. Una de ellas es empezar los partidos restando. Repitió el guión con su rival chino y le salió perfecto. 'Break' de entrada. La mediática Eugenie Bouchard, ahora comentarista de televisión, viralizó un comentario referido a la camiseta sin mangas del tenista: “Te quiero Carlos, pero hay que tapar ese pezón”. Alcaraz le hizo caso y jugó con una camiseta blanca por debajo de su elástica. El chino llegó a remontar un 3-1. Recordaba, por momentos, la mejor versión de Kei Nishikori. Sin embargo, claudicó después ante un ser superior. El guión se repitió en el segundo set. Del 2-0 favorable al español se pasó al 3-3 y pelota de rotura para Wu. La razón había que buscarla en el 30 por ciento de puntos ganados con el segundo servicio y en las dobles faltas. Tampoco ayudaban los 11 errores no forzados de derecha que molestaban en sobremanera a Alcaraz. Carlitos, que mejora el porcentaje de victorias en los grandes del Big Three —94 partidos ganados por 13 perdidos—, no pierde en un major desde la final de Wimbledon 2025 contra Jannik Sinner. El italiano se ha perdido el torneo neoyorquino por una lesión de rodilla y Alexander Zverev, el primer cabeza de serie, se empeña en dejarse sets en cada uno de sus partidos. Ha disputado 10 en dos rondas frente a Lorenzo Sonego y Quentin Halys. Eso traducido en tiempo son nueve horas y 26 minutos. El primer cabeza de serie en el camino de Alcaraz será este domingo Tommy Paul, vigésimo cabeza de serie y que se ganó el billete tras ganar en cinco mangas a Alexander Bublik.

On Friday, Carlos Alacaraz defeated Yibing Wu in straight sets to move one step closer to repeating as US Open champion.

In the women's draw, Aryna Sabalenka cruised to victory, while Jessica Pegula outlasted Leylah Fernandez in a three-set thriller.

Carlos Alcaraz defeated Yibing Wu in straight sets to march on to the Round of 16.

The defending champion was far from his best, struggling to stay consistent on his forehand and find his first serve.

This wasn't a total surprise considering he's coming off a four-month layoff with a wrist injury.

Despite the up-and-down performance, there is little reason for concern for the Spaniard, who is still the favorite to win the US Open.

In other action, Tommy Paul avenged his US Open loss against Alexander Bublik last year in a five-set thriller.

After losing the first set, Bublik hit another gear, dominating to win the next two sets.

However, Paul was undeterred and played flawlessly through the final two sets, while Bublik suffered a massive dip in focus.

The third round of the US Open continues Saturday on ESPN, with all matches also being available on ESPN Unlimited.

Zizou Bergs (31) vs. Botic Van De Zandschulp

Alexander Zverev (1) vs. Alejandro Tabilo (25)

Match of the Day: Learner Tien (14) vs. Jakub Mensik (17)

Learner Tien is seeking to become the youngest American man to reach the Round of 16 at the US Open since Andy Roddick in 2002.

The 20-year-old enters the third round on the heels of an impressive victory over Gael Monfils.

But the challenge is about to get significantly tougher with Jakub Mensik looming.

When his serve is on, Mensik can be an incredibly difficult opponent to face.

The 21-year-old is the slight underdog against Tien but certainly has what it takes to advance in New York.

That being said, the clear physical edge goes to Tien, and if he's able to make this a physical match, he should be expected to prevail.

Aryna Sabalenka defeated Kamilla Rakhimova in the third round, keeping her quest for a third consecutive US Open title alive.

Sabalenka opened up the match in dominant fashion, winning her first 16 points on first serve.

Rakimova settled into a rhythm in the second set before Sabalenka broke at 4-4 to serve out the match.

The world No. 1 played her trademark aggressive tennis, hitting 29 winners, along with 10 aces.

articles.title: Aryna Sabalenka halts US Open match to speak to umpire about someone smoking weed: 'It's so strong'
articles.summary: Despite the distraction, Sabalenka easily dispatched Kamilla Rakhimova in straight sets to advance to the Round of 16.
articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka is moving on to the Round of 16 at the US Open — but not before experiencing an unexpected disruption. On Friday, Sabalenka had to pause the match to address what she believed was someone smoking marijuana in the stands.

Early in Sabalenka's third-round win over Kamilla Rakhimova, the World No. 1 appeared to look at her box and confirm that they also could smell the smoke. Sabalenka then walked over to the umpire's chair to ask if she could get them to stop.

"Someone is smoking weed," Sabalenka could be heard telling the umpire. "Do you mind? Because it's so strong."

The umpire appeared to signal to someone about the issue by miming the smoking with her fingers.

Sabalenka went on to win the match, 6-3, 6-4. Overall, Sabalenka dominated Rakhimova, trailing just twice in the match and winning the last three games of the second set to take the victory.

Postgame, Sabalenka was lighthearted about the stoppage. In response to a reporter's question about "how much of a high" she was on in this tournament, Sabalenka joked that she misinterpreted the question at first because she "can only hear weed stuff."

As for the smoking itself, Sabalenka said that it was windy enough that the smell may have traveled outside the stadium. Still, she requested that the culprit reconsider smoking near the action.

"I was like, guys you can do whatever. You can smoke, whatever. You can relax as much as you can. But please don't do it around the tennis courts," Sabalenka said. "It's a bit tricky to handle that smell while you're trying to compete at your best.

The interruption is just the latest in a tournament that has been seemingly overrun by influencers . Some have caused disruptions , including during Naomi Osaka's first-round match, leading Osaka to later encourage the newcomers to "read up" on tennis etiquette.

So far in these early rounds, Sabalenka is winning everything pretty handily, and has now won all three of her matches in straight sets. That's a good thing, since the stakes are higher for the Belarusian player: Though Sabalenka has held her current No. 1 ranking since October 2024, the 28-year-old is being heavily challenged for her title.

As things stand, No. 2-ranked player Elena Rybakina needs only to make the US Open semifinals in order to take the top overall ranking.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz beats Wu Yibing to reach fourth round, Daniil Medvedev through
articles.summary: Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz underlines his US Open title credentials by sweeping aside Wu Yibing to reach the fourth round as the draw opens up further.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz swept Wu Yibing aside to reach the US Open fourth round - and said he is getting better with every match as he continues his return from a long-term injury lay-off.

The Spaniard underlined why he remains a serious contender to defend his title in New York with a 6-3 6-4 6-1 victory over China's Wu.

The 23-year-old's opening-round match in Flushing Meadows was his first on a singles court for 139 days after injuring his wrist in April.

Alcaraz came through his opener in straight sets but had to battle back from a set down against Portugal's Jaime Faria in the second round.

However, Alcaraz continued to build momentum on Friday, needing two hours and 20 minutes on court to beat Wu.

"To be honest, I'm better than I thought," the seven-time major champion said.

"Physically I thought I was going to be bad after the first match, but I am recovering really well. I am doing great things off the court to be in a good state.

"Right now, I think my level is really good. I think I have caught the rhythm of the competition.

"Every time that I step on the court I give it all. I'm just trying to improve, be better every match and I think I'm getting there."

American 20th seed Tommy Paul - who Alcaraz has beaten six times in a row - awaits in the fourth round.

Alcaraz's path to an eighth major title has opened up over the past few days.

French Open champion and Wimbledon runner-up Alexander Zverev heads the men's draw in the absence of injured world number one Jannik Sinner.

As the second seed, Alcaraz cannot meet Zverev until the final - and the German has been taken to five sets and kept on court until 2am in his two matches so far.

Novak Djokovic suffered a shock first-round exit to Argentine Mariano Navone, while Canadian third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime lost to Karen Khachanov in the second round.

As it stands, American eighth seed Ben Shelton is the only top-10 player that Alcaraz can meet before the semi-finals. He could then face seventh seed Daniil Medvedev in the last four.

Alcaraz has won all three of his meetings with Shelton and has a 6-3 winning head-to-head against Medvedev - although the inconsistent Russian beat him at Indian Wells in March.

Meanwhile, Zverev's potential pre-final opponents include home hope Taylor Fritz and Italy's French Open runner-up Flavio Cobolli.

'It's so strong' - Sabalenka halts play over cannabis smell

100 influencers invited to US Open spark debate on 'tennis etiquette'

'Alcaraz more of a favourite with each win'

While Alcaraz at times appeared frustrated with his own inconsistency against Wu, the former world number three continues to demonstrate progress.

Alcaraz landed 21 winners as he extended his career-best streak of Grand Slam singles match wins to 17, but that was counteracted by 33 unforced errors and a first-serve success rate of just 67%.

Despite a seemingly straightforward scoreline, Alcaraz did not have it all his own way and repeatedly made his feelings clear on the court.

He surrendered early advantages in the first two sets - his first serve dipped to 53% in the second set - but managed to reset to avoid further complications.

"Every win Alcaraz gets, he is becoming more of a favourite," former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Four months off, no matches and win the US Open? He is a class above everybody else, when he is good, and he is getting better by the moment.

"The way he is moving, there is no reason for him not to do well."

Former champion Medvedev also progressed on Friday, overcoming French 26th seed Arthur Rinderknech 6-4 6-4 6-4.

Medvedev achieved his sole major title at the US Open in 2021, and has won 21 of his 23 singles titles on hard courts.

He appears in the form to challenge again, on the evidence of his three straight-set victories so far, but will have to overcome American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe or Monaco's 22nd seed Valentin Vacherot next.

Britons Henry Patten and Joe Salisbury both won their men's doubles first-round matches.

Top seeds Patten and Finnish parner Harri Heliovaara won 6-4 6-2 against Argentine brothers Francisco and Juan Manuel Cerundolo, while Salisbury and American Rajeev Ram beat Australian John-Patrick Smith and Mexico's Santiago Gonzalez 7-6 (7-3) 7-6 (8-6).

Jan Choinski and Bulgaria's Alexander Donski also advanced with a 7-6 (7-5) 6-4 win over American pair Martin Damm and Mackenzie McDonald.

articles.title: Serena Williams Says She Doesn't 'Have an Agenda' For Tennis Return Amid US Open Run
articles.summary: Serena Williams told Emily Rella of People Magazine in an exclusive interview that she doesn't have an "agenda" as she continues her return to professional tennis at the U.S. Open.
articles.body:
Serena Williams told Emily Rella of People Magazine in an exclusive interview that she doesn't have an "agenda" as she continues her return to professional tennis at the U.S. Open.

"I really don't have an agenda right now. I'm taking it one match at a time and seeing where my body can take me," Williams told Rella. "It's been exciting to see what I'm capable of and to feel myself getting stronger. Right now, I'm just enjoying being back out there and seeing where it goes."

Williams has won 23 Grand Slam singles titles and 14 Grand Slam doubles championships during her legendary career. In an Aug. 2022 essay for Vogue , Williams announced that she was "evolving away from tennis" to focus on growing her family and continuing the progress of her venture capital firm, Serena Ventures.

Williams got back on the court in June for doubles action at the HSBC Championships in London. She won her first match alongside partner Victoria Mboko against the No. 3 seed, Nicole Melichar-Martinez and Erin Routliffe. Their run ended in the quarterfinals via walkover after Mobko suffered a left knee injury during her singles action at the tournament.

Williams played doubles in Berlin in June and Cincinnati in August. She also made her singles return at Wimbledon, giving Maya Joint a great fight before losing in three sets.

Now Williams has made her return to the U.S. Open. She played mixed doubles with Carlos Alcaraz. The duo won their first match in straight sets against Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool before falling to the No. 4 seed (and the eventual finalists), Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli.

A reunion with sister Venus Williams, a seven-time Grand Slam singles winner and 14-time Grand Slam doubles champion (all with Serena), now awaits in women's doubles. The duo is scheduled to face the No. 14 seed, featuring Joint and Hao-Ching Chan, on Friday.

articles.title: Coco Gauff Addresses Influencers Disrupting Matches at US Open After Naomi Osaka Interruption
articles.summary: Coco Gauff weighed in on social media influencers disrupting US Open matches following an interruption during Naomi Osaka's first-round match.
articles.body:
Coco Gauff weighed in on social media influencers disrupting US Open matches following an interruption during Naomi Osaka's first-round match.

"I think it's great to have a different demographic to the sport," Gauff told reporters on Thursday, via People's Skyler Caruso . "I have no problem with influencers. I've met some of them and follow some of them online."

"Luckily the ones I do follow online do follow the etiquette and know tennis pretty well," she added.

Gauff explained how some actions of influencers, particularly flash photography, have bothered her during matches.

"I definitely think no flash photography because that does bother [me]. I am one of the lenient players," Gauff said, per Caruso. "Try not to talk too loud. I mean, Ashe is a very loud court, so I'm used to it, but definitely not like mouthing TikToks and stuff in the middle of a point."

"It's not just for the rest of the players but for the viewing experience for those around," she added. "If I had to pick noise over flash, I definitely think no flash because that actually does mess us up a little bit."

During Osaka's first-round clash with Anastasia Zakharova, umpire Kader Nouni paused play to ask guests to limit their distractions.

Osaka ended up defeating Zakharova before taking down Kateřina Siniaková in the second round.

Gauff has also punched her ticket to the third round of the US Open, winning over Zeynep Sönmez and Paula Badosa in straight sets.

Her next match takes place against Cristina Bucșa on Saturday.
